buckets.name: No grid power at home
frequency_sentences: Of 100 households like yours, about 35 (25–75) will lose grid power for a day or more in the next 10 years.
Being ready for 3 days leaves about 8 (6–25) of 100 households like yours facing a longer power cut in the next 10 years.
This number mostly depends on how often windstorms happen where you live (expert estimate) and how long power cuts from a windstorm bigger than any in the recent records last (expert estimate).

buckets.name: Tap water must be treated
frequency_sentences: Of 100 households like yours, fewer than 1 will have to boil or treat their tap water for a day or more in the next 10 years.
At the setting you chose (1 in 100 years), this is rare enough that there is no target.

buckets.name: No tap water at all
frequency_sentences: Of 100 households like yours, about 75 (65–95) will have no usable tap water for a day or more in the next 10 years.
Being ready for 2 months leaves about 8 (2–25) of 100 households like yours facing a longer water outage in the next 10 years.
This number mostly depends on how often droughts happen where you live (expert estimate) and how long water outages from drought lowering a well last (expert estimate).
Your well pump runs on electricity, so every power cut is also a water cut. The pump itself also fails now and then (about once in 14 years).

buckets.name: Can't get to a store
frequency_sentences: Of 100 households like yours, about 50 (25–85) will be unable to shop for food and supplies for 3 days or more in the next 10 years.
Being ready for 10 days leaves about 9 (4–30) of 100 households like yours facing a longer stretch without shopping in the next 10 years.
This number mostly depends on how long times without shopping from store shortages and runs on stores last (expert estimate) and how often pandemics happen where you live (expert estimate).

buckets.name: Dangerous heat or cold indoors
frequency_sentences: Of 100 households like yours, about 25 (20–60) will face dangerous heat or cold at home with no working cooling or heating for a day or more in the next 10 years.
Being ready for 3 days leaves about 6 (4–20) of 100 households like yours facing a longer spell of dangerous heat or cold in the next 10 years.
This number mostly depends on how often windstorms happen where you live (expert estimate) and how long power cuts from a windstorm bigger than any in the recent records last (expert estimate).
Your heating needs electricity to run (a gas furnace needs it for the igniter and fan), so a long winter power cut also cuts your heat.
A power cut during a heat wave also stops your air conditioning.

The 22-mile (35 km) trip is about 7 hours on foot; carry about 4 litres of water for it in hot weather.
The get-home bag is sized by the walk home at about 3 miles an hour, with about half a litre of water per hour in hot weather.

requirements.plain: 4 battery lights: a headlamp or lantern for each person aged 4 and over. Use lights, not candles. (Ready.gov; some amounts are estimates)
1 pack of AA or AAA batteries for the lights and the radio: one pack lasts a household about 7 days. Check which sizes your lights use. (Ready.gov; some amounts are estimates)

Your generator burns about 2.8 gallons of fuel a day at light load (up to 7.1 gallons at full load): 3 days is about 8.4 gallons. Store it in approved cans, no more than 10 in an attached garage and none indoors. Use stored fuel within 6 months. Run the generator outdoors only, at least 20 feet from windows, doors and vents. (Generator spec sheet, local fire code, CDC, Ready.gov)

1 battery power station (about 1,070 Wh each) as an optional upgrade for lights, phones and a radio. Your essential load (phones) is about 45 Wh a day, 140 Wh for 3 days; one station gives about 910 Wh after losses, enough for about 20.2 days of that load. A full-size fridge alone would drain one in about 0.9 days. (retail prices, ENERGY STAR; some amounts are estimates)

A portable generator that can start your well pump, so your 12 large animals have water after the first 3 days of a power cut; it runs the fridge and lights too. Starting a pump takes 2 to 3 times its running watts (about 1,250 W): check the pump's nameplate before you buy. It must run outdoors, at least 20 feet from windows, doors and vents, never in a garage, and it needs fuel (see the fuel line). (CDC, Ready.gov, ASPCA; some amounts are estimates)

Optional: keeping a fridge running takes about 995 Wh a day (a chest freezer about 597) × 3 days = 2,990 Wh. A closed fridge keeps food cold about 4 hours and a full freezer about 48; shelf-stable food avoids the need. (ENERGY STAR, Ready.gov)

Optional: your well pump needs about 1,250 W to run (1,000 to 1,500) and 2 to 3 times that to start; check its nameplate. At 1 hour a day that is 3,750 Wh for 3 days. A battery power station usually cannot start it; a generator or a hand pump can. Stored water is the cheaper way to cover this. (an estimate)

5 people × 1 gallon a day × 14 days = 70 gallons, plus 4.1 gallons for pregnancy or breastfeeding, plus 11.4 gallons for the 2 dogs and the 3 cats: about 85.4 gallons. Replace water you store yourself every 6 months. Your target is 60 days. Storing all of it would take about 366.2 gallons, so the plan stores the first 14 days and makes the rest safe with a filter and a water source (see the next line). (Ready.gov, CDC, National Academies, PetMD; some amounts are estimates)

Free first step: fill clean drink bottles you already have with tap water, about 6 gallons, the most a household can usually gather this way. Not milk jugs: they leak. Label them and replace the water every 6 months. (Ready Reckoner research, CDC, Ready.gov, Church of Jesus Christ; some amounts are estimates)

After day 14, for the other 46 days: make about 6.1 gallons of water safe each day, about 280.7 gallons in all, with a water filter and a source such as rain barrels, a stream or a pond, instead of storing more. Filter it, then boil it for 1 minute (3 minutes above 5,000 feet), or add 8 drops of 6 % unscented bleach per gallon (6 drops of 8.25 %) and wait 30 minutes; double the bleach for cloudy or very cold water. If there is no water source near you, store more water instead. (Ready.gov, CDC, National Academies, PetMD; some amounts are estimates)

1 bottle of plain unscented bleach (5 to 9 % sodium hypochlorite, not the splashless kind), for making water safe and for cleaning, however long your target is. At about 0.5 mL a gallon, each ounce treats about 60 gallons of clear water (30 if it is cloudy or very cold), so one bottle treats thousands of gallons. Bleach weakens in storage: buy a fresh bottle every 6 months, when you replace the water you store yourself. (CDC, EPA; some amounts are estimates)

12 large animals × 25 L a day (20 to 30) × 3 days = 900 L, about 237.8 gallons. Fill tubs or stock tanks before a storm or an outage. Your target is 60 days; store the first 3 days, until the generator runs the well pump, and in a longer power cut let it keep the pump going (see the generator line) instead of storing weeks of water. A drought that lowers the well is different: plan to haul water in, and a stock tank holds what you haul. (Sphere, ASPCA; some amounts are estimates)

Instead of relying on the generator, you could store 14 days for the animals in stock tanks: 12 large animals × 25 L a day × 14 days = 4,200 L, about 1,109.5 gallons of tank space. A stock tank also holds water you haul in. (Sphere, ASPCA, BYU, Church of Jesus Christ; some amounts are estimates)
A two-bucket toilet for when toilets can't flush: 2 sturdy buckets with a seat, one for pee and one for poo. (RDPO, Oregon OEM)

Toilet bags: about 0.45 heavy garbage bags a person a day (0.3 to 0.6), counting both bags of a double-bagged load: 5 people × 60 days = 135 bags. Fill halfway, tie, double-bag, and store away from food, water, children and pets. Don't put them in curbside trash or bury them unless officials say so. (RDPO, Oregon OEM; some amounts are estimates)

Cover material for the poo bucket (sawdust, shredded paper, dry leaves or pet bedding): about 1 cup a person a day (0.5 to 1.5) × 5 people × 60 days = 300 cups, about 18.8 gallons. (RDPO; some amounts are estimates)

2 adults at about 2,262 kcal a day each, 1 teen at about 2,280 kcal a day, 1 child aged 4 to 12 at about 1,667 kcal a day and 1 toddler at about 1,067 kcal a day, plus 400 for pregnancy or breastfeeding: about 9,937 kcal a day × 10 days = 99,400 kcal. These are moderately active needs; the form does not ask sex, so men's and women's needs are averaged. Count calories, not servings. (Dietary Guidelines)

As everyday groceries: about $401 for 50 person-days (USDA Thrifty Food Plan, $8.44 a person a day, minus 5 % for a household of 5). Buy what you already eat, keep it in the pantry and use the oldest first. (USDA)

As bulk staples such as wheat, rice and beans: about $125 ($2.15 to $2.85 a person a day). Cheapest, but it needs cooking and is short on some vitamins, so it suits months rather than days. (Church of Jesus Christ, BYU)

As freeze-dried or dehydrated meals: about $1,192 ($9 to $39 per 2,000 kcal, so $447 to $1,938). They need about 0.6 gallons of extra water a person a day to prepare. (Dietary Guidelines, retail prices; some amounts are estimates)

A retail "30-day" food kit supplies about 1,290 to 1,730 kcal a day. For the average person here (about 1,987 kcal a day) one lasts about 19 to 26 days, not 30. Compare kits by total kcal. (Dietary Guidelines, retail prices)

Dry food for the 2 dogs and the 3 cats for 10 days (at least a week): about 0.7 lb a day for each dog and 0.15 lb a day for each cat = 18.5 lb. Feed what the label says for yours, and keep it in an airtight, waterproof container. (ASPCA, Ready.gov; some amounts are estimates)
Food for the 2 dogs and the 3 cats for 10 days (50 pet-days, at least a week): what they eat now, in an airtight, waterproof container. (ASPCA, Ready.gov)

If you cook or boil water on a camp stove: about 0.2 lb of fuel a person a day × 5 people × 10 days = 10 lb, or 20 canisters of 0.5 lb each. Use it outdoors only, never indoors (carbon monoxide). (CDC, Ready Reckoner research, EIA, retail prices; some amounts are estimates)
Toilet paper: about 1 roll a person every 5 days × 5 people × 60 days = 60 rolls. Better still, measure a week's use and double it for two weeks. (Oregon OEM; some amounts are estimates)
Soap for 5 person-months: 5 people × 1 month. Each is 250 g of bathing soap and 200 g of laundry soap, about 2,250 g in all. (Sphere)

Period products for 2 cycles each, about 20 products a cycle (15 to 30). The form doesn't ask sex, so the plan counts half of the 2 people aged 13 to 64 who are not pregnant or nursing: 2 cycles' worth, about 40 products. Keep soap, clean underwear and pain relievers with them, and put used products in a separate bag. (CDC, Sphere, Oregon OEM; some amounts are estimates)
Diapers: about 6 a day for each toddler still in diapers, × 10 days = 60 diapers. Keep at least one large pack on hand. (CDC; some amounts are estimates)
Baby wipes: at least 2 packs for each child in diapers for up to 2 weeks: 2 packs. (CDC)

2 battery fans: 1 for the home plus 1 for the 1 person most at risk from heat (65 and over, babies, pregnancy). Fans help only while it is below 90 °F indoors; above that, go to a cooling centre. (CDC; some amounts are estimates)
5 cooling towels, one for each person: wet them and wear them on the neck in a heat wave. (an estimate)
A heat plan: find your nearest cooling centre (dial 2-1-1), pick the coolest room, cover sunny windows, and agree who checks on whom. Never leave people or pets in a closed car. (CDC, Ready.gov)
5 warm blankets, one for each person: most homes already have them. (Ready.gov, Sphere)
5 sets of warm layers (coat, hat, gloves, dry socks), one for each person. (Ready.gov, CDC)
An upgrade, not a need: 5 sleeping bags or extra heavy blankets, one for each person. Blankets and warm layers cover a cold target of 3 days. (Ready.gov, Sphere; some amounts are estimates)

A cold plan: pick one room to keep warm, close off the others, put towels under doors and cover windows at night. Never heat with a gas oven, grill, camp stove or generator indoors (carbon monoxide). Gas, oil and propane furnaces usually need electricity for their fans and controls, so plan for cold without power. A body temperature below 95 °F needs medical help at once. (CDC; some amounts are estimates)

No antibiotics are included in this plan. If you have a specific, foreseeable need, such as remote travel, talk to your own clinician about a standby prescription with written instructions. Never use fish or pet antibiotics, never share prescriptions, and don't use expired ones. (CDC, FDA)
1 person carries an epinephrine auto-injector: check the expiry date, and ask the prescriber how many to keep at home, in the go-bag and on the person. (Ready.gov)
1 battery or hand-crank radio that gets NOAA Weather Radio, with a tone alert, for warnings when phones and power are down. (Ready.gov, NOAA)
Power banks: 3 phones × about 15 Wh a day (10 to 20) × 3 days without power = 140 Wh. Text instead of calling to save battery. (Ready.gov; some amounts are estimates)

3 two-way radios for the 3 people aged 13 and over, to reach each other when phones are down. FRS radios need no licence; GMRS radios reach farther but need a $35 FCC licence that covers the family for 10 years. (FCC; some amounts are estimates)
4 written contact cards, one for each person aged 4 and over: an out-of-area contact, meeting places and key numbers. Phones die; paper does not. (Ready.gov)
1 paper map of your area, marked with meeting places and ways out. Save offline maps on your phone too. (Ready.gov)

Cash in small bills, kept with your documents, because ATMs and cards may not work in an outage: about $100 to start, or enough for about 3 days of basics (food, fuel, medicine) at your own daily spending. No agency gives a dollar amount. (Ready.gov, FEMA; some amounts are estimates)

4 go-bags, one for each person aged 4 and over (babies' things go in a parent's bag): a sturdy bag you already own will do. Pack copies of documents, a phone charger, cash, a flashlight, a whistle, a change of clothes and sturdy shoes, and add water, food and medicines from your home supplies rather than buying them twice. You may get only minutes of warning (a local tsunami or a fast fire), so keep the bags packed by the door, and one at work if you work in a danger zone. Practise grabbing them and leaving. Plan where you would stay for about 2 days. (Washington EMD, Ready.gov, CDC; some amounts are estimates)

Water for the go-bags comes out of the water you store at home, not on top of it: the Red Cross three-day supply for leaving home, about 5.3 gallons a day for the 5 people × 2 days = 10.6 gallons. Keep it with the bags or take it as you leave. If you leave on foot, carry what you can (about 2.5 L each) and a filter; the rest goes in the car. (Red Cross, Washington EMD, Ready.gov, CDC; some amounts are estimates)

Food for the go-bags comes out of your home food supply, not on top of it: about 9,937 kcal a day × 2 days = 19,900 kcal of food that needs no cooking or refrigeration. (Red Cross, Washington EMD, Dietary Guidelines)

5 pet carriers, one for each pet, with a pet go-kit: water and food from your home supplies, any medicine each takes, records and a photo. Public shelters may take only service animals, so find pet-friendly places to stay ahead of time. (ASPCA, Ready.gov)

Water for the pet go-kit, set aside from your stored water rather than bought extra: 7 days for the 2 dogs and the 3 cats = 5.7 gallons. Replace it every 2 months. (ASPCA, PetMD, Merck Veterinary Manual; some amounts are estimates)
Food for the pet go-kit, set aside from your pet food rather than bought extra: 10 days (7 to 10 days) for the 2 dogs and the 3 cats = 50 pet-days. Replace it every 2 months. (ASPCA)
Keep both vehicles at least half full at all times, and fill up when leaving looks likely. (Ready.gov)

Person 2 travels 21.7 miles (35 km) by car to work or school; walking home at about 3 mph takes about 7.2 hours. Keep a get-home bag in the car: comfortable walking shoes, a light, a paper map, cash in small bills, a rain or warm layer, and water and snacks from home. Be ready to stay at work for 24 hours if you can't leave. (FHWA, Ready.gov; some amounts are estimates)

Water for person 2's walk home: 7.2 hours × about 0.5 L an hour = 3.6 L, in a bottle filled from home rather than bought extra. Past about 2.5 L, carry a filter or purification tablets and an empty bottle instead of all the water. (FHWA; some amounts are estimates)

Snacks for person 2's walk home: about 800 kcal for 7.2 hours on foot (about 1,250 kcal every 12 hours), from your food at home rather than bought extra. (FHWA, Dietary Guidelines; some amounts are estimates)
2 car emergency kits: jumper cables, a flashlight, warm clothes, a blanket, bottled water and snacks; sand or cat litter in snow country. (Ready.gov)

2 family first-aid kits for 5 people: the Red Cross list for a family of 4 (bandages, gauze, tape, antiseptic wipes, gloves, a breathing barrier, a cold pack, tweezers, an emergency blanket and a thermometer). Add your own medicines and emergency numbers, and replace what you use. (Red Cross)

1 package of each of 4 kinds of non-prescription medicine (a pain reliever, an anti-diarrhea medicine, an antacid and a laxative): one package of each lasts about 14 days for 4 people. That is 4 packages for 10 days. Follow the label, and ask a pharmacist about children's versions. (Ready.gov, Red Cross; some amounts are estimates)

N95 masks for wildfire smoke or an outbreak: 1 a day for each of the 4 people aged 4 and over, for 5 days = 20 masks. A well-fitting N95 protects more than a cloth or surgical mask. (CDC, Ready.gov; some amounts are estimates)
1 oral thermometer (non-mercury, non-glass; it is on the Red Cross kit list). (Red Cross)

Oral rehydration salts for vomiting, diarrhea or heat illness: 3 packets a person for every 2 weeks, at least 2 weeks' worth. For 5 people and 14 days that is 15 packets. Mix each packet into 1 litre of safe water. (CDC; some amounts are estimates)

A fire escape plan: two ways out of every room, a meeting spot outside, and a practice run with everyone. If anyone sleeps upstairs, check that each bedroom has a second way out, such as a window onto a porch roof or an escape ladder. Test your smoke alarms every month. (Ready.gov)
Swap phone numbers with 2 neighbours and agree who checks on whom after a storm or an outage, when phones and roads may be down. (an estimate)

Savings goal: about 6 months of expenses ($31,200 at $5,200 a month), built up over time and kept apart from the supplies budget. You have about 1 month saved now. Planners often suggest 3 to 6 months; the CFPB says it depends on your situation. (FINRA, St. Louis Fed, CFPB)

Copy the 4 parts of FEMA's Emergency Financial First Aid Kit: IDs, financial and legal papers (including insurance), medical information, and household contacts. Keep copies in a waterproof, fire-resistant place or with someone you trust, with photos of your home and belongings, and update them once a year. (FEMA)

Home and renters policies usually don't cover floods. Decide on flood insurance before you need it: a new policy usually starts 30 days after you buy it. It pays up to $250,000 for the building and $100,000 for belongings. (FEMA, FloodSmart, Ready.gov)

# Your preparedness packet

**For:** 2 adults, 1 teenager, 1 child and 1 toddler, with 2 dogs, 3 cats and 12 large animals  
**Where:** Ellis County, Kansas  
**Home:** an owned house on rural land, with a basement, a private well, propane heat and central air conditioning  
**Plan date:** October 1, 2026  
**Ready for:** very serious disruptions, the kind that come about once in 100 years (the 1-in-100 setting), in today's climate. Water is planned at the basic level, about 1 gallon a person a day.[1]

## Summary

**Where you are now:** getting started. **What is enough for your risks:** three months of supplies; each need stops at the step that covers it. At your budget, the plan gets there by month 34 (August 2029).

### The three things that matter most

1. Of 100 households like yours, about 35 (25–75) will lose grid power for a day or more in the next 10 years. Be ready to manage about 3 days at home with no power, and about 2 months with no tap water.
2. Of 100 households like yours, about 50 (25–85) will be unable to shop for food and supplies for 3 days or more in the next 10 years. Keep about 10 days of food you normally eat.
3. Of 100 households like yours, about 20 (10–45) will have an income gap of more than 3 months in the next 10 years. Losing a paycheck is the longest disruption most households face. Aim for about 6 months of expenses in savings over time, apart from this supplies budget.

### Start here

These cost nothing and come first. This month's 8 free steps are all under Your plan.

- [ ] Epinephrine: carry two auto-injectors and keep them in date
- [ ] Tap water in clean reused bottles
- [ ] Keep medicines going: a written list, early refills, an emergency supply

### What the plan assumes you already have

- [x] A charged mobile phone: alerts, calls and a backup light (3 phones)
- [x] Go-bag for each person: a backpack you pack from your supplies (4 bags)
- [x] Manual can opener (1 opener)
- [x] A cooking pot with a lid (1 pot)
- [x] Three days of the food you normally eat (5 × 3 days of food for one person)
- [x] A warm blanket for each person (5 blankets)
- [x] Warm layers for each person: a coat, hat and gloves (5 sets)
- [x] Towels to wet and cool down (5 towels)

Most homes have these, so the plan does not ask you to buy them. If any is missing, untick "Assume everyday basics" on the Have screen, or list the item as not owned, and the plan will add it.

## Your risks

The events most likely to reach a household like yours in Ellis County, Kansas, over the next 10 years, most likely first. A lost job or a week-long outage is far more likely than a disaster from the movies, and the plan is ordered the same way.

### The ones most likely to reach you

#### 1. Medical emergency

Nearly every household like yours will have someone need emergency care in the next ten years (about 2.4 times a year).[2, 3]

**What helps.** Take a first-aid and bleeding-control class. You may be able to save a life by acting right after an injury, before help arrives.[4] Keep a stocked first-aid kit. Check it regularly and replace anything used or out of date.[5] Keep a list of each person's medicines, doses and allergies with your emergency supplies.[6] Know how to reach 911. Call if you can, and text where that service works.[7] Set up telehealth with your own clinician before you need it.[8]

**What to avoid.** Do not start antibiotics on your own or take someone else's. The wrong medicine can delay the right treatment and cause serious side effects.[9] Do not use expired medicines.[10]

**What it can do:** a medical emergency. **How bad:** Serious. **How sure:** Based on data.

#### 2. Heat wave

Nearly every household like yours will go through a heat wave in the next ten years (about 1.6 times a year).[11, 12]

**What helps.** Know where you can go to cool off. Dial 2-1-1 to find air conditioning near you.[13] Cover windows with drapes or shades, and weather-strip doors and windows.[14] Take cool showers, wear loose, light-colored clothing, and drink plenty of fluids. Check on family members, older adults and neighbours.[14] Heat can cause power outages, so plan for refrigerated medicines and powered medical devices.[13] In a drought, follow local limits on water use, and make saving water a daily habit.[15]

**What to avoid.** Do not rely on a fan when it is over 90°F indoors. It can make you hotter.[13] Never leave people or pets in a closed car on a warm day. Heat stroke is an emergency. Signs include a body temperature above 103°F, hot, red, dry skin, a fast pulse and confusion. Call 911.[14]

**What it can do:** no power and dangerous heat or cold at home. **How bad:** Serious. **How sure:** Mostly data.

#### 3. Strong wind

Nearly every household like yours will lose power or have damage in a windstorm in the next ten years.[12, 16]

**What helps.** Pick your shelter spot now. A safe room or storm shelter is best. The next best is a small, windowless room or basement on the lowest floor of a sturdy building.[17] Sign up for your community's warnings, and learn what your sirens sound like.[17] Know the signs of a tornado: a rotating funnel cloud, a cloud of debris, or a roar like a freight train. In your shelter, protect your head and neck with your arms, and pile blankets or cushions around you.[17] When thunder roars, go indoors. Get into a building or a car with a roof.[18]

**What to avoid.** Stay away from windows, doors and outside walls.[17] There is no safe place in a car during a tornado, only less dangerous ones. If you are caught, stay buckled in and keep your head below the windows.[17] During a thunderstorm, avoid running water and electronics plugged into the wall.[18]

**What it can do:** no power, no phone, internet or card payments and damage to the home. **How bad:** Moderate. **How sure:** Rough data.

#### 4. Stranded in a vehicle

Of 100 households like yours, about 95 (63 to nearly all) will be stranded away from home by a crash, breakdown or shutdown in the next ten years.[12, 19]

**What helps.** Keep a car kit with jumper cables, sand, a flashlight, warm clothes, blankets, water and snacks.[20] Keep the gas tank at least half full.[21] Check the pressure in all your tires, including the spare, at least once a month.[22] Before a winter trip, tell someone where you are going and when you expect to arrive, and ask them to call for help if you are late.[23] If you drive an electric car, know its range and where you can charge along your route.[24, 25]

**What to avoid.** If you are stuck in a snowstorm, staying in the car is often safest. Tie a bright cloth to the antenna. Run the engine about 10 minutes an hour with a window open a little, and keep the exhaust pipe clear of snow.[23] Never drive into a flooded road or around the barriers.[26]

**What it can do:** being stranded away from home. **How bad:** Minor. **How sure:** Mostly data.

#### 5. Job loss

Of 100 households like yours, about 95 (87–99) will have someone lose a job in the next ten years.[12, 27, 28]

**What helps.** Build an emergency fund a little at a time. The right amount depends on your situation.[29] Planners often suggest three to six months of living expenses, and more if your income varies.[30] Know how to file for unemployment in your state.[31] Keep copies of your financial, legal and medical papers together, with the names of people to call.[32] Write a bare-bones budget you could switch to, and keep a pantry that can stretch a tight month.

**What to avoid.** File soon after losing work: contact your state's unemployment program as soon as you can.[31] Do not keep your emergency fund in investments you would have to sell. A savings account lets you take money out at any time without a penalty.[30]

**What it can do:** lost income. **How bad:** Serious. **How sure:** Mostly data.

#### 6. Supply chain disruption

Of 100 households like yours, about 86 (63–98) will find store shelves empty of things they need in the next ten years.[12]

**What helps.** Keep extra food that needs no refrigeration, cooking or water, and choose foods your family will eat.[33] Use the oldest cans first and replace them as you go.[34] Buy a little at a time. Ready.gov asks people to buy supplies slowly, so everyone can get what they need.[35] Keep a manual can opener.[33] The plan counts food in calories, not servings. Many "30-day" meal kits hold only about 1,300 to 1,700 calories a day.[36] That is less than most adults need.[37] Store food somewhere cool and dry. Below 85°F is best.[34]

**What to avoid.** Do not buy everything at once. It strains your budget and the store. Do not buy or eat from cans that bulge, leak, are rusted or are deeply dented.[34] Do not trust a kit's "days" label. Check the calories on the package instead.

**What it can do:** no way to get to a store and gaps in medicine. **How bad:** Minor. **How sure:** Expert estimate.

### No grid power at home: about 3 days (up to 7 days)

**What helps.** Have a flashlight for each person.[53] Keep a battery or hand-crank radio, and a backup battery for each phone.[54] Keep the fridge and freezer closed. A closed fridge keeps food cold for about four hours, and a full freezer for about two days.[53] If someone relies on a powered medical device or cold medicine, make a plan with their medical provider now.[53] You can also ask your power company to put you on its list for priority restoration.[6] A battery power station burns no fuel, so it makes no carbon monoxide.[55]

**What to avoid.** Never run a generator inside your home or garage, even with the doors and windows open. Keep it outside, more than 20 feet from windows, doors and vents.[55] Put a carbon monoxide alarm on every level of your home.[53] Never heat your home with a gas stove or oven. Unplug electronics, because the power can come back with a surge that damages them.[53]

### No tap water at all: about 2 months (3 weeks to 6 months)

**What helps.** Store at least one gallon per person per day, for drinking and keeping clean.[1] Fill clean bottles or jugs with tap water and replace it every six months.[56] You can pick a level in the plan. About 3 liters a day covers drinking to survive, one gallon is the basic default, and about 4 gallons (15 liters) is the humanitarian minimum for drinking, cooking and washing.[57] A tank water heater holds 20 to 80 gallons of clean water.[58, 59] For long outages, a filter and a source of raw water go further than more jugs.[52] Filters do not remove viruses, so add a disinfectant such as chlorine dioxide after filtering.[60] A two-bucket toilet keeps waste safe when toilets cannot flush.[61]

**What to avoid.** Do not store water in containers that held chemicals.[56] Milk jugs seal poorly and turn brittle.[62] Never drink pool or spa water. Use it only for washing and cleaning.[59]

### Can't get to a store: about 10 days (7 days to 3 weeks)

**What helps.** See "Supply chain disruption" under Your risks.

### Dangerous heat or cold indoors: about 3 days (2–7)

**What helps.** Agree who checks on whom, especially older neighbours and anyone who lives alone.[13, 23] In heat, go where there is air conditioning. Dial 2-1-1 to find one.[13] Cover windows with drapes or shades.[14] In cold, close off rooms you don't need, stuff towels under doors, and cover windows with blankets at night. Have extra blankets, sleeping bags and warm coats.[23] Babies under one year old should never sleep in a cold room.[23]

**What to avoid.** Fans move air but do not lower body temperature.[14] Above 90°F indoors, a fan can make you hotter.[13] Never heat your home with a gas oven, and never use a grill or camp stove indoors.[55] Keep space heaters 3 feet from anything that can burn.[63] Never leave people or pets in a closed car on a warm day.[14]

### Medication and medical-supply continuity: about 2 weeks (7 days to 1 month)

**What helps.** Refill early, while you still have a week left. The Red Cross suggests keeping a 7-day supply, and Florida advises at least two weeks.[64, 65] People with diabetes should pack supplies for at least 1 to 2 weeks.[66] Talk to your doctor or pharmacist about building an emergency supply, and keep a written list of each person's medicines, doses and allergies.[6] Many states let pharmacists give an emergency refill, but the rules differ from state to state.[67] After a declared disaster, a federal program can help people without insurance replace prescriptions.[68] If a medicine must stay cold, ask how long it can be kept warm, and plan a cooler.[53]

**What to avoid.** If the power is out for more than a day, throw away medicine that should be refrigerated, unless the label says otherwise.[53] Keep insulin cool but never frozen.[69] Do not use expired medicines. Weak antibiotics can fail to treat an infection.[10] Do not share antibiotics or save them for later.[9]

### No phone, internet or card payments: about 3 days (2–7)

**What helps.** Turn on emergency alerts on every phone. They are free, and you do not need to sign up.[70] Keep a battery or hand-crank radio and a NOAA Weather Radio with a tone alert.[54] NOAA Weather Radio has more than 1,000 transmitters covering all 50 states.[71] Write important phone numbers on paper, not only in your phone.[72] Pick an out-of-state contact everyone can text, and a place to meet if you are separated.[73] Keep some cash in small bills, because ATMs and credit cards may not work.[74] License-free two-way radios (FRS) let family members talk over short distances without a phone network.[75]

**What to avoid.** Do not rely on one source of news. Do not assume you can text 911 everywhere. It is not available in every area, so call 911 if you can.[7]

**What helps.** See the steps under Family plan.

**What to avoid.** Many people wait to check with others before they act on a warning.[76] Always follow the instructions of local officials, and leave early enough to avoid being trapped by bad weather.[21] Never walk or drive through floodwater. Six inches of moving water can knock you down.[77]

### House fire

**What helps.** Put smoke alarms inside and outside sleeping areas and on every level of your home. Test them every month.[78] Make an escape plan with two ways out of each room, and practice it twice a year.[79] Cooking left alone is the top cause of kitchen fires that spread beyond the pan, so stay with your cooking. Keep a pan lid or baking sheet nearby to cover a pan that catches fire.[80] Keep anything that can burn at least 3 feet from heaters, fireplaces and candles.[63] A multipurpose extinguisher labeled "A-B-C" works on most home fires.[81]

**What to avoid.** If a person or pet is still inside, get out, call 911, and tell firefighters where they are.[79] Never heat your home with an oven.[63] Turn off space heaters when you leave the room or go to bed.[63] Replace 9-volt alarm batteries at least once a year.[78]

### Home and personal security

**What helps.** Burglars look for homes that are easy targets. Lock up, and light the places where someone could hide.[82] Work with your neighbours to look out for each other.[82] Protect key accounts with a password manager and two-step login.[83] Learn a simple way to handle a tense moment: notice what is happening, say hello, judge the risk, and get help if you need it.[84] If an attack happens in a public place, getting away is the top priority.[85]

**What to avoid.** After a disaster, be careful with people who show up offering fast repairs or help for a fee. Report scams at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.[86] Do not hide a spare key under the doormat or a planter. Leave it with a trusted neighbour.[82]

- **Make a household plan and a contact card for each person.** Agree how you will reach each other, where you will meet if you are separated, and who picks up the children (Ready.gov). ### Leaving home: triggers and routes

About 6 of 100 households like yours have to leave home quickly at least once in 10 years. Warning can be 1 minute to 12 hours ahead. Plan to be away for about 2 days.[11, 12, 38, 43, 44]

- **Plan how you would leave: zone, routes, destination and triggers.** Look up your evacuation zone and routes on your state and county emergency management websites, mark two routes on a paper map, and pick where you would go, pet-friendly if you have pets (Ready.gov). For each likely hazard, write a go-or-stay card and an if-then trigger, such as 'If our zone gets an evacuation warning, we leave within 30 minutes.' Plans written in if-then form make people more likely to follow through.[21, 54, 76, 97, 98, 99, 100, 101]
- **Keep your vehicle ready: half a tank, a charged battery, a good spare.** Keep at least half a tank of gas at all times and a full tank when an evacuation looks likely (Ready.gov); if you drive an electric car, keep it charged through storm season and pick destinations within its range (Hillsborough County, Florida). Check the spare tire with the others each month, and keep a phone charging cable in the car (NHTSA). Run the engine only outdoors, never in a garage (CDC).[20, 21, 22, 24, 25, 55, 88, 102]

- **Practice: ten-minute drills and the first things to do.**

#### Drills and if-then plans

**If-then plans.** An if-then plan links a trigger to an action: "If the county issues an evacuation warning for our zone, we leave within 30 minutes." Plans written this way help people follow through.[100] When a warning comes, people often wait to confirm it with others before they act.[76] A trigger you agreed on earlier leaves less to decide in the moment. Write one for each likely hazard, and add who picks up the children and where you will meet.[94]

**Drills.** In New Zealand, people who took part in earthquake drills knew the right actions better, used them more during real shaking, and did more to prepare.[103] Among people who got out of the World Trade Center on 9/11, those with earlier emergency training were less likely to develop PTSD.[104] Practice your fire escape plan twice a year.[79] Other ten-minute drills: Drop, Cover and Hold On, a night without power, grabbing the go-bag against a timer, and sealing a room to shelter in place.[101]

**What to avoid.** Do not skip drills because they feel silly. Each one you finish counts toward your plan.

### School, work and getting home

The household plan above covers school, daycare and work plans and a walking route home. Each commuter's get-home bag is under Checklists.

#### Talking with children about emergencies

**Before anything happens.** Let children help build the kit and practice the plan.[105] Make sure each child knows your family meeting place and has a contact card.[94] Practice the fire escape plan together twice a year.[79]

**When something happens.** Start by asking what they already know and what questions they have. Give simple, concrete facts without scary details. For a young child, that might be: "A tree branch fell on the power lines, so the lights are off." Tell them about the many people working to help, and the steps being taken to keep them safe.[106]

**What to avoid.** Limit news coverage. If children watch, watch with them and answer their questions.[106] Reassure them when you honestly can, but do not give false reassurance. Let them know it is all right to be upset. If you feel overwhelmed, get support from another adult first. Helping others in the community can ease a child's sense of helplessness.[106]

### Neighbors

- **Neighbours and skills: swap numbers, check on each other, learn first aid.**

#### Neighbours and mutual aid

**The gap.** About 7 in 10 people expect help from friends and family in a disaster, but fewer than 2 in 10 had heard how to help their neighbours.[107]

**What helps.** Swap phone numbers with two neighbours. Agree who checks on whom, especially older neighbours and anyone who lives alone. Make a simple contact list for your street. Give a trusted person a spare key, and tell them where your supplies are and how to use any medical equipment.[108] Host a block party, since strong communities start with prepared neighbours.[109] Take CERT training to learn fire safety, light search and rescue, and disaster first aid.[110]

**What to avoid.** Meet the people next door before you need them. A short hello now makes it easier to knock on a door later.

### Pets

- **Pet plan: microchip, records, a photo and a buddy.** Keep your pet's ID tag and microchip details current, put vaccination records and a recent photo with your documents, and arrange a buddy who can care for or evacuate your pets if you cannot (Ready.gov). If officials ask you to evacuate, your pets should go too.[98, 99]
- **Plan for horses and livestock.** Plan to evacuate large animals early, set up a buddy system with nearby farms to share trailers and pasture, and keep vet records handy (ASPCA). Large animals need about 20 to 30 liters of water a day each, so fill tubs before the power goes out (Sphere).[57, 99]

## Documents and money

Keep paper copies in a waterproof pouch and photos you can reach from any phone. FEMA's Emergency Financial First Aid Kit groups them in four parts.[32]

- [ ] **Who you are:** photo IDs, birth certificates, Social Security cards, passports, and pet records.
- [ ] **Money and legal papers:** insurance policies, the lease or deed, bank and card contact numbers (not PINs), and recent tax returns.
- [ ] **Medical papers:** insurance cards, the written medicine list, prescriptions, and vaccination records.
- [ ] **Contacts:** family, doctors, the insurance agent, the landlord or lender, and employers.

- **Documents and insurance: copy key papers, record belongings, check cover.** Use FEMA's Emergency Financial First Aid Kit to gather IDs, financial and legal papers, insurance, medical information and contacts, and photograph or video every room and valuable item. Keep paper copies in a waterproof bag and another copy with someone you trust or in secure online storage (FEMA). Check what your insurance covers: standard home and renters policies do not cover flood or earthquake damage, a new flood policy usually takes 30 days to start, and renters can buy their own policy and contents-only flood cover (Ready.gov, FEMA).[32, 54, 73, 74, 77, 107, 111, 112]
- **Fire-resistant, waterproof document pouch.** A fire-resistant, water-resistant pouch or small case for paper copies of key documents, a USB drive and some cash, easy to grab when you leave (FEMA's financial kit suggests fire- and waterproof storage).[32, 93]

### Insurance questions

- Home and renters policies usually don't cover floods. Decide on flood insurance before you need it: a new policy usually starts 30 days after you buy it. It pays up to $250,000 for the building and $100,000 for belongings. (FEMA, FloodSmart, Ready.gov)[74, 111, 112]

### Cash

- Cash in small bills, kept with your documents, because ATMs and cards may not work in an outage: about $100 to start, or enough for about 3 days of basics (food, fuel, medicine) at your own daily spending. No agency gives a dollar amount. (Ready.gov, FEMA; some amounts are estimates)[12, 16, 32, 74, 88]

### Savings

Of 100 households like yours, about 20 (10–45) will have an income gap of more than 3 months in the next 10 years. The goal is about 6 months of expenses (about $31,200); you have 1 month saved. Your supplies plan is done by month 34. After that, your $80 a month for supplies could go here, reaching the goal in about 27 years. This is a savings goal, kept separate from the supplies budget.

- **Money: start an emergency fund and a bare-bones budget.** Set up an automatic transfer, however small, into a savings account you keep for emergencies; the CFPB says the right amount depends on your situation, and planners often suggest working toward three to six months of expenses (FINRA). Write down your essential monthly costs and what you would cut first, so you know how far savings would stretch. If anyone earns, find your state's unemployment website now, so you could file right away if a job ends (Department of Labor).[27, 29, 30, 31, 113, 114]

## Special needs

### Medicine

- 1 person carries an epinephrine auto-injector: check the expiry date, and ask the prescriber how many to keep at home, in the go-bag and on the person. (Ready.gov)[6]

- **Keep medicines going: a written list, early refills, an emergency supply.** Write a paper list of each person's medicines with the dose their prescriber set, allergies, and the prescriber's and pharmacy's numbers, and keep copies in the go-bag and with your documents (Ready.gov). If anyone takes a daily medicine, refill when a week is left and ask the prescriber and pharmacist how to build an emergency supply; some states allow emergency refills, and a federal program can help people without insurance after a disaster. Set up telehealth and pharmacy logins now, and put spare glasses in the go-bag (Ready.gov).[6, 8, 10, 32, 54, 64, 67, 68, 115]
- **Epinephrine: carry two auto-injectors and keep them in date.** Anyone prescribed an epinephrine auto-injector should always carry two, because one dose may not be enough (FDA-approved patient information). Check the expiry dates, replace a used one right away, and show family, caregivers and teachers where they are and how to use them. Ask the prescriber how many to keep at home, at school and in the go-bag.[6, 116]

### Antibiotics

- No antibiotics are included in this plan. If you have a specific, foreseeable need, such as remote travel, talk to your own clinician about a standby prescription with written instructions. Never use fish or pet antibiotics, never share prescriptions, and don't use expired ones. (CDC, FDA)[9, 10, 117, 118]

### Babies and toddlers

- Diapers: about 6 a day for each toddler still in diapers, × 10 days = 60 diapers. Keep at least one large pack on hand. (CDC; some amounts are estimates)[12, 16, 41, 42, 88, 119, 120]
- Baby wipes: at least 2 packs for each child in diapers for up to 2 weeks: 2 packs. (CDC)[12, 16, 41, 42, 119, 120]
- 1 oral thermometer (non-mercury, non-glass; it is on the Red Cross kit list). (Red Cross)[5]

### Pregnancy and nursing

- **Plan for pregnancy and nursing.** CDC advises people who are pregnant or nursing to keep at least 7 to 10 days of prescriptions and ask about a 30-day emergency refill, keep copies of prenatal records, and avoid water treated with iodine. Learn the urgent warning signs of pregnancy and after birth, and where you would go to give birth if your hospital is closed.[60, 115, 121]

### Pets and animals

- 12 large animals × 25 L a day (20 to 30) × 3 days = 900 L, about 237.8 gallons. Fill tubs or stock tanks before a storm or an outage. Your target is 60 days; store the first 3 days, until the generator runs the well pump, and in a longer power cut let it keep the pump going (see the generator line) instead of storing weeks of water. A drought that lowers the well is different: plan to haul water in, and a stock tank holds what you haul. (Sphere, ASPCA; some amounts are estimates)[11, 12, 57, 88, 99]
- Dry food for the 2 dogs and the 3 cats for 10 days (at least a week): about 0.7 lb a day for each dog and 0.15 lb a day for each cat = 18.5 lb. Feed what the label says for yours, and keep it in an airtight, waterproof container. (ASPCA, Ready.gov; some amounts are estimates)[12, 16, 41, 42, 88, 98, 99, 120]
- 5 pet carriers, one for each pet, with a pet go-kit: water and food from your home supplies, any medicine each takes, records and a photo. Public shelters may take only service animals, so find pet-friendly places to stay ahead of time. (ASPCA, Ready.gov)[21, 99]
- Water for the pet go-kit, set aside from your stored water rather than bought extra: 7 days for the 2 dogs and the 3 cats = 5.7 gallons. Replace it every 2 months. (ASPCA, PetMD, Merck Veterinary Manual; some amounts are estimates)[88, 99, 122, 123]
- Food for the pet go-kit, set aside from your pet food rather than bought extra: 10 days (7 to 10 days) for the 2 dogs and the 3 cats = 50 pet-days. Replace it every 2 months. (ASPCA)[99]

### Stress and mental health

#### Stress, mental health and the 988 line

**What helps.** Save 988 in every phone. It offers free, judgment-free support 24/7 for mental health, substance use and more, by call, text or chat.[124] After a disaster, the Disaster Distress Helpline offers crisis counseling 24/7 to anyone in emotional distress. Call or text 1-800-985-5990.[125] Write a short calm plan: what you might feel, what helps you, and who you will call.[101] Oregon's 2 Weeks Ready program even includes practicing mindfulness as a step in getting prepared.[126]

**What to avoid.** Do not keep the news on all day. No one, adult or child, benefits from graphic details or disturbing images.[106] Reach out before things feel unbearable. The 988 line supports people in emotional distress as well as in crisis.[124]
